items.title: The morning after: what December’s IMO vote means for a fixture
items.original_title: The morning after: what December’s IMO vote means for a fixture
items.summary: Whatever the IMO decides in December, a broker will price a dry bulk trip the next morning. The vote changes which line of that fixture carries the carbon, and how much. The framework was approved in April 2025 and its adoption adjourned for a year last October; it was debated again at MEPC 84 in the spring. From 2028 every tonne of fuel burned on international voyages counts, wherever the ship trades, against two targets: a ship pays $100 for each tonne of CO2-equivalent between the direct-compliance line and the base line, and $380 for each tonne above the base line. On the Rotterdam trip, assuming no change to the European rules, that adds roughly €29,000 in 2028, taking the carbon on the fixture to about €96,000, or €1.45 a tonne and 12% of the hire. For the broker, the practical point is less the price of a tonne of carbon than its allocation. If the framework is adopted, every fixture acquires a carbon line, not only those touching Europe, and the charter party has to say who carries it. On a time-charter trip, the BIMCO clauses written for the EU ETS and FuelEU do not by themselves cover an IMO remedial unit.

items.title: QatarEnergy Continues LNG Buying Spree to Hedge Future Hormuz Disruptions
items.original_title: QatarEnergy Continues LNG Buying Spree to Hedge Future Hormuz Disruptions
items.summary: DOHA, Oct 29 (Reuters) – QatarEnergy is buying long-term supplies of liquefied natural gas from the US and other producers as part of a trading strategy designed to generate revenue if exports through the Strait of Hormuz are disrupted in the future, CEO Saad Sherida Al-Kaabi told Reuters on Thursday. “In a scenario where you have a closure of the strait, which is the true contingency that we’re looking to have, you’d immediately see a spike in gas price and you’ll be able to generate revenue for QatarEnergy that otherwise wouldn’t be generated,” Kaabi, who is also the minister of state for energy affairs, said of the plan. Kaabi’s remarks reveal for the first time how Qatar, one of the world’s largest LNG producers, plans to offset lost income from the Iran war and protect revenue against future disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz. QatarEnergy believes it can leverage its fleet of about 200 LNG tankers, the world’s largest, as well as QatarEnergy Trading, which Kaabi said will soon become the world’s largest gas trading platform. The hedge targets a market transformed after Iran responded to a war launched by the US and Israel on February 28 by effectively closing the Strait of Hormuz, a vital chokepoint through which a fifth of the world’s oil and LNG shipments pass.

items.original_title: Shell and Total Post Highest Quarterly Profit Since 2022
items.summary: LONDON, Oct 29 (Reuters) – Shell and TotalEnergies reported on Thursday sharply higher third-quarter profits and raised share buybacks, as war-driven energy prices and record refining margins helped both beat expectations. Shell raised its quarterly buyback to $5 billion from $3 billion, the second-largest buyback on record, while Total reiterated plans to buy back $2.5 billion of shares in the fourth quarter and said it would buy back another $2.5 billion in the first quarter of 2027. The shareholder distributions offer an insight into how oil majors plan to spend the profits generated by the US-Israeli war with Iran, which is in its ninth month and has disrupted global energy supplies. Also on Thursday, Austria’s OMV reported its highest quarterly operating profit since 2022. Refining margins nearly quadrupled for both Shell and Total compared with a year ago. They reached $42 a barrel and $33.2 per barrel, respectively, helping to boost earnings to the highest since 2022, when Shell delivered a record $6 billion buyback program. Shell posted third-quarter net profit of $10.81 billion, above analysts’ average estimate of $10.33 billion and almost double the $5.43 billion it earned a year earlier. Total also took a $1.9 billion impairment mainly tied to offshore wind and a South Korean petrochemical stake.

items.original_title: Tanker feared sinking off Oman after reported projectile strike
items.summary: A tanker has reportedly been left burning and largely submerged following a suspected projectile strike in the Strait of Hormuz, with UK maritime authorities confirming reports of a vessel on fire off the Omani coast. Maritime security firm Vanguard said the incident occurred approximately 9 nautical miles north of Khasab, on Oman’s Musandam Peninsula. The master of a passing Panama-flagged tanker reported seeing the unidentified vessel on fire and mostly underwater, raising concerns that it may have sunk or be in the process of sinking. The British maritime security centre has not independently confirmed that the vessel was struck by a projectile or that it is sinking. There has also been no confirmation of casualties or whether any crew members have been evacuated. The latest incident comes amid continued attacks on commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, with tankers and other merchant vessels repeatedly targeted during the ongoing US-Iran confrontation. Several attacks in recent months have resulted in the loss of vessels, including the bulk carrier Cape Dao, which sank after being struck off Khasab in September, and the containership GFS Pride, lost in the strait earlier this month. The International Maritime Organization’s latest figures show 121 confirmed maritime incidents across the Middle East this year as of October 27, with 24 seafarer fatalities recorded.

All 18 crew members, comprising 14 Filipinos and four Ukrainians, were rescued by Bulgarian naval and border police vessels and taken to Varna. The three NATO members condemned the attacks and agreed to strengthen maritime intelligence sharing and early-warning arrangements. The latest incidents follow a succession of deadly strikes against merchant shipping off Romania and Bulgaria this month, including the October 23 sinking of Khoryv near Constanta, which left one seafarer dead and three missing.

items.title: Where are all the crew needed going to come from?
items.original_title: Where are all the crew needed going to come from?
items.summary: Shipping has never been short of ambition. The orderbook proves it. But increasingly, the industry again needs to ask itself the uncomfortable question: where are all the crew coming from? Today the physical risks are becoming impossible to ignore. My advice is simple: either manage your crew yourself, or go to where professional crew management is genuinely practised and get involved. The crew should feel that they belong to the owner, not merely to a management company. All too often, supposedly dedicated crew are taken from one owner’s pool and deployed to another owner’s vessel(s) when the manager has an urgent requirement — particularly where immediate matrix or tanker-compliance requirements need to be satisfied. There is simply no manager existing today of the scale and with the reserves of quality crew to take over management of say a large fleet of tankers without taking existing crew from other dedicated pools. Because the next generation of ships may be built of steel, composites, software and sophisticated technology, but without the right people on board, they are simply very expensive assets sitting idle in the water or trading dangerously and unsafely.

items.summary: Italian terminal operator Contship is getting back into the liner business, sealing a deal to acquire Italian shipping and logistics group Tarros through its subsidiary Sogemar, in a deal aimed at creating a major integrated transport network across the Mediterranean. The transaction covers the entire Tarros group, including its shipping operations, port handling businesses and inland logistics activities. Financial terms have not been disclosed. Founded in 1828, Tarros operates a door-to-door network spanning 16 countries and 31 ports, connecting European markets with North Africa and other Mediterranean destinations. The group employs 751 people and serves approximately 2,700 customers. The acquisition includes Tarros SpA and its overseas subsidiaries, Terminal del Golfo, Car Box, Compagnia Marittima Servizi and Med Logistics Malta. Contship intends to combine Tarros’s regional shipping services with Sogemar’s intermodal network and its existing terminal operations in Italy, Egypt and Morocco. The deal represents a significant consolidation of Mediterranean shortsea shipping and logistics operations, bringing together complementary maritime, terminal and inland transport networks. The acquisition remains subject to regulatory approvals, with completion expected during the fourth quarter of 2026.

items.summary: A CMA CGM containerships waits at anchor outside the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach. The joint Clean Marine Fuel Feasibility Assessment , conducted as part of the ports’ Green Shipping Corridor initiatives, examined which alternative fuels shipping companies are most likely to adopt, how demand could develop through 2030, and what investments would be needed to support bunkering operations. The study estimates that annual LNG demand at the San Pedro Bay ports could reach between 65,000 and 115,000 metric tons by 2030, while methanol demand could range from 64,000 to 250,000 metric tons, depending on market conditions and the deployment of alternative-fuel vessels. The report also acknowledges that the environmental benefits of alternative marine fuels depend heavily on how they are produced and sourced. In April, the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach renewed their Green and Digital Shipping Corridor agreement with Singapore, with the partners committing to advance alternative-fuel bunkering, demonstration projects and digital connectivity.

items.summary: UK logistics groups welcomed the decision in today’s new budget to maintain a 5p-per-litre fuel duty cut and avoid planned increases, and ensuring warehouse rates do not rise, but there have also been warnings that businesses continue to face significant cost pressures. items.title: Tariff anouncements cause cargo chaos for box terminals, says TiL
items.original_title: Tariff anouncements cause cargo chaos for box terminals, says TiL
items.summary: Sudden tariff announcements, not tariff levels themselves, trigger costly cargo surges that terminals cannot absorb, delegates at TOC Americas in Cartagena were told. Rather than destroying container trade, said TiL Group’s director for terminal investments in North America, Tom van Eynde, tariffs were relocating it, pointing to cargo shifting from Canadian ports into TiL’s US terminals as evidence. “It has been somewhat of a wild ride over the past year, the past two years,” Mr van Eynde noted, referring to tariffs in the US being introduced and then cancelled. “They’re not really reducing the trade flows, they’re just relocating them.” While the terminal operator saw a reduction in certain trade flows to the US through Canadian ports, he said these were then automatically being picked up by TiL terminals in US ports. Expecting the situation to be “a temporary thing”, Mr van Eynde said he expected disruption to settle once tariffs hit a range of 10% to 15% – “at that kind of level we see very little impact anymore on the volume.” The real damage, he said, came less from the tariffs themselves than from sudden announcements that triggered a rush of cargo before a deadline, only for conditions to return to normal once it passed.

The uptick in Chinese purchases suggests demand ahead of the northern winter is outweighing price concerns. items.title: New study pours cold water on nuclear shipping economics
items.original_title: New study pours cold water on nuclear shipping economics
items.summary: The commercial case for nuclear-powered shipping remains highly uncertain, with new research suggesting the technology could become competitive by 2040, but only with dramatic reductions in reactor costs and effective global carbon regulation. A study published today by University College London’s Energy Institute examines the total cost of ownership of nuclear-powered containerships, comparing them with conventionally fuelled and ammonia-powered alternatives. A conventional containership costs $119.6m in the model, compared with $148.5m for an ammonia dual-fuel vessel. The nuclear equivalent ranges from $228m under optimistic assumptions to $582m for first-of-a-kind reactor technology. The researchers calculate that reactor production costs would need to fall by as much as 80% for nuclear propulsion to become commercially attractive, reductions that have yet to be demonstrated. Under the most favourable assumptions, nuclear becomes the cheapest propulsion option from 2040, but only when the IMO’s proposed Net-Zero Framework is included, allowing nuclear vessels to earn revenue from surplus emissions credits. The study also challenges the argument that nuclear propulsion could transform container shipping economics by allowing vessels to travel considerably faster. The central question is who will finance the expensive first generation of nuclear ships before the economies of scale needed to make the technology competitive materialise.

items.summary: Seven Japanese companies have joined forces to build four ammonia-fuelled car carriers and establish an integrated bunkering network, in one of the most ambitious commercial shipping projects yet involving the alternative fuel. Nippon Yusen Kaisha (NYK) and Kawasaki Kisen Kaisha (K Line) will each operate two vessels, scheduled for delivery in 2030, with Japanese shipbuilders Imabari Shipbuilding, Shin Kurushima Dockyard and Nihon Shipyard responsible for their design and construction. The vessels, Japan’s first ammonia-fuelled car carriers, will feature dual-fuel engines and sufficient ammonia tank capacity to undertake transpacific voyages without switching fuels. They are expected to transport vehicles for customers including Toyota. Kyokuyo will construct a dedicated ammonia bunkering vessel, also scheduled for completion in 2030, which will be owned and operated by NYK or one of its subsidiaries. NYK and K Line will establish an equally owned joint venture to market and supply the fuel, primarily through ship-to-ship bunkering at Nagoya and Mikawa. The partners describe the initiative as the world’s first integrated commercial ammonia marine fuel supply chain linking procurement, bunkering infrastructure and vessel operations. The new car carriers will incorporate multiple layers of protection against ammonia leaks, including detection and neutralisation systems, reflecting the fuel’s toxicity and corrosiveness. The announcement follows Japan’s first ship-to-ship ammonia bunkering operation to an ammonia-fuelled vessel in September, led by NYK.

items.original_title: The EU is showing how regional maritime rules can support a global framework at the IMO
items.summary: In April 2025, governments at the International Maritime Organization (IMO) agreed on a historic global regulation, the Net-Zero Framework (NZF). It was designed to set global shipping on a course to net-zero by 2050 in a just and equitable way. Global shipping is responsible for around 3% of global emissions annually, roughly as much as the economies of Germany or Japan. While T&E analysis has previously shown that the NZF in itself is not strong enough to reduce shipping emissions at the pace countries agreed to, the agreement set an important global standard for a sector so far exempt from most climate rules. The EU is clear that if the IMO establishes a carbon pricing scheme such as the NZF, a ship sailing internationally will not have to pay double for the same emissions under the EU ETS. The newly proposed “ETS as a service” would allow EU trade partners to raise revenues on their own 50% shares through the EU’s existing system, without the administrative burden of setting up their own ETS from scratch. Now, the EU is opening a path for its regional rules to co-exist with a global framework and involving others in the benefits.

The 130-meter China Zorrilla , built by Australian shipbuilder Incat Tasmania for ferry operator Buquebus, completed its first commercial crossing between Buenos Aires, Argentina, and Colonia, Uruguay, on October 22. The system powers eight electrically driven waterjets, making China Zorrilla the largest battery-electric vessel ever constructed. The start of commercial service follows an official ceremony in Buenos Aires on October 21, attended by Incat Managing Director Craig Clifford, Buquebus representatives, and maritime authorities and government officials from Argentina and Uruguay. “This ship proves that large, high-capacity commercial vessels can operate on electric power,” Clifford said. Its entry into service demonstrates the growing potential for battery-electric technology in high-capacity ferry operations, particularly on fixed routes where shore-based charging infrastructure can support regular crossings. The Tasmanian shipbuilder is currently building three 129-meter battery-electric ferries for Danish operator Molslinjen, along with two 78-meter hybrid-electric vessels at its Hobart facility. items.title: Shipping cuts training when it needs it most
items.original_title: Shipping cuts training when it needs it most
items.summary: Irene Rosberg, who runs the Blue MBA at Copenhagen Business School, returns to Splash today. When business conditions become difficult, training is often one of the easiest budgets to cut. In shipping, that is becoming an increasingly dangerous habit. There is a contradiction here because shipping wants better leaders, more skilled seafarers and managers capable of making increasingly complex decisions, but those capabilities do not simply appear when they are needed. This is why I find the tendency to reduce training when companies come under financial pressure so short-sighted. Lifelong learning cannot be a phrase we use in speeches while treating the training budget as expendable when margins tighten. It also means recognising that the future leaders of shipping may come from broader professional backgrounds than they did previously. Shipping will spend enormous sums preparing its fleets for the future. It should be equally serious about preparing the people who will be expected to lead them.

items.summary: The orderbook for pure car and truck carriers (PCTCs) has surged amid booming Chinese vehicle exports and elevated charter earnings, raising concerns that an expanding fleet could outpace demand as European restrictions on Chinese vehicle imports threaten to curb a key source of cargo growth. Greek brokerage Intermodal said last week that 82 PCTCs were contracted in the first nine months of 2026, compared with just nine vessels ordered throughout 2025 and a 10-year annual average of 35 vessels. The orderbook-to-fleet ratio has consequently risen to 26%, well above its historical average of 14%, pointing to a substantial expansion in carrying capacity over the coming years. Fuelling the surge in newbuilding orders is the growth in Chinese vehicle exports, which totalled 8.2m units in the first nine months of 2026, up 66% year-on-year. China’s rapidly expanding automotive exports have kept charter rates elevated, with ships being fixed for $95,000 per day, near levels last seen in 2024. Domestic NEV sales contracted by 9.4% year on year, reinforcing the industry’s reliance on exports to absorb production. In October 2026, the EU and China reportedly reached a preliminary understanding on proposed restrictions covering Chinese-built conventional and plug-in hybrid vehicles.

items.title: Congestion-induced ‘double sailings’ cancel out Golden Week blanks
items.original_title: Congestion-induced ‘double sailings’ cancel out Golden Week blanks
items.summary: Deployed capacity on the transpacific and Asia-Europe trades during this year’s Golden Week holiday was the highest on record, according to new analysis from Sea-Intelligence. Port congestion in Asia, caused by a succession of typhoons, led to vessel bunching at loading ports, and subsequently resulted in a series of “double sailings”, which cancelled out carriers’ blanking strategy during the holiday period when they typically look to skip voyages due to a lack of cargo sitting on Asia’s docks “Double sailings are essentially two departures on a liner service in a week,” analysts at Sea-Intelligence said. “Liner services work on weekly departure frequencies – ie, one vessel departs the origin region every week. “When vessels get delayed, they bunch up – the delayed departure that moved from week 1 to week 2 is now sailing along with the original week 2 departure, hence a ‘double sailing’,” the consultancy explained. This meant deployed capacity during the Golden Week period – which Sea-Intelligence defined as taking place between weeks 40 and 42, to account for the lag in inland transport work unable to take place because drivers were on holiday – was this year higher on the transpacific and Asia-Europe trades than ever before.

items.summary: Norwegian chemical tanker owner Odfjell has reportedly sold two 2011-built vessels for more than $62m as it continues reshaping its fleet. Shipbrokers identified the 46,098 dwt Bow Elm and 46,047 dwt Bow Lind as having been sold together, with the deal agreed on a surveys-passed basis. Both vessels were built at South Korea’s SLS Shipbuilding and belong to Odfjell’s coated tanker fleet. The ships have been trading in Odfjell’s chemical and product tanker operations since entering service in 2011. Odfjell’s latest published fleet register, covering June 30, lists both vessels as owned tonnage. In April, Odfjell agreed to acquire four 40,000 dwt stainless-steel chemical tanker newbuildings from a Japanese owner in a deal worth approximately $290m. The vessels are being built at Kitanihon Shipbuilding and are scheduled to enter Odfjell’s fleet between 2027 and 2029. Its wider programme encompasses more than 20 newbuildings, including owned and chartered vessels, as it increases the proportion of modern, fuel-efficient ships in its deepsea fleet. The latest reported sale would remove another two vessels approaching 15 years of age while releasing more than $62m in gross sale proceeds.

items.title: Asia Pacific the star performer as airfreight rates take off
items.original_title: Asia Pacific the star performer as airfreight rates take off
items.summary: Surging jet fuel prices have added to the upward pressures that have seen global airfreight rates climb above the highs of the previous two peak seasons, as the industry enters its busiest period of the year. Figures from the latest TAC-compiled Baltic Air Freight Index and World ACD indicate that rates have been rising by between 4% and 4.7% over the past fortnight, up some 26% compared with the same period of 2025. Covering the period from 12-18 October, WorldACD noted chargeable weight and available capacity was up 2% week on week, with carriers having opted to expand freighter operations following two consecutive weeks of reductions. TAC said the index had already surpassed the highs recorded over the previous two peak seasons in the run-up to both Thanksgiving and Christmas, with jet fuel prices having a part to play after more than doubling year on year, up 113%, said IATA. The index noted that together with fuel increases, disruption thrown up by conflicts in Europe and the Middle East was creating a floor for airfreight rates, and that carrier s were not prepared to sink beneath that in a dash for volumes.

items.summary: Monaco-based Transocean Maritime Agencies has ordered two 50,000 dwt chemical and product tankers at China’s Guangzhou Shipyard International (GSI), adding another vessel type to its expanding newbuilding programme. The CSSC-controlled yard recently signed the contract, marking its first order from a Monaco-based shipowner. Transocean is a family-controlled shipping company established in the 1960s by the late Guenther Neunhoeffer. The company, led by Ruth McLoughlin, operates a fleet of around 15 vessels, primarily comprising bulk carriers and tankers. In October 2025, the Monaco owner emerged as the buyer behind two-plus-two 1,930 teu feeder newbuildings at Guangzhou Huangpu Wenchong Shipbuilding, scheduled for delivery in 2028. Shipbuilding sources have also linked the company to another two 3,100 teu containerships at New Dayang Shipbuilding. Transocean previously ordered two 64,000 dwt ultramax bulkers at New Dayang in 2024, continuing a fleet expansion strategy spanning several Chinese yards. The latest contract adds to a busy period for GSI in the MR tanker segment. The Guangzhou yard has recently attracted orders from Geneva-based Advantage Tankers and Greek owner Top Ships.

items.title: Transworld gets green light for $43m boxship deal

items.summary: India’s Transworld Shipping Lines has secured shareholder approval for the $42.78m acquisition of two containerships from another company within its controlling shareholder’s group, clearing a key hurdle in its ongoing fleet restructuring. The Navi Mumbai-based listed owner disclosed in a filing that shareholders had backed the purchase of the 2006-built OEL Surya and OEL Varun from Orient Express Lines Inc. The transaction will be carried out through Transworld Sea-Connect IFSC, a wholly owned subsidiary of the shipping company. The 2,748 teu OEL Surya is valued at $22.03m, while the 2,478 teu OEL Varun carries a price tag of $20.75m. Both acquisitions were originally approved by Transworld’s board on September 7, subject to shareholder consent and any other necessary approvals. The two vessels are already commercially employed, providing Transworld with an existing income stream as it brings the tonnage onto its subsidiary’s books. The move follows a series of disposals and acquisitions as Transworld reshapes its vessel portfolio. Earlier this month, the company agreed to acquire the 2011-built, 55,648 dwt supramax Saltwind Explorer for $16.5m.In September, it struck a $9.25m deal to sell the 2011-built bulker TBC Kailash to Mandarine Ocean, following several containership disposals to DP World-controlled Avana Logistek.

With our agentic AI, all those booking requests no longer need to be handled manually.” The forwarder did not outline what percentage of automation was expected, and Mr Neill acknowledged: “We have more work to do automating all the steps for booking, but this is already a major leap forward.” Its pricing agents have determined and delivered more than 80,000 quotes for over 3,600 customers. Mr Short made rather a sweeping claim for CH Robinson’s position: “With our maturity in using AI to augment our talented experts, only CH Robinson is equipped to transform something as complicated as freight forwarding.” The firm argues that faster processing brings practical advantages for shippers trying to secure capacity or respond to disruption. CH Robinson claims a 23% reduction in time spent on the affected work, with brokers focusing on validation and compliance.

items.title: China-India rates ease but port delays still a strain on services
items.original_title: China-India rates ease but port delays still a strain on services
items.summary: Rates for containers moving from China to India have begun to cool as seasonal import demand, associated with India’s festival-driven consumption, loses momentum. New data secured by The Loadstar points to a 10%-20% decline in spot rates for bookings from major Chinese load ports to India, particularly JNPA (Nhava Sheva) on the west coast and Chennai on the east. For example, Indian importers are now able to book a 40ft shipment from Shanghai to JNPA at about $3,200 per box, down from about $3,800 a month ago. Hong Kong-JNPA rates are currently in the region of $3,600/40ft, down from $3,800 a month ago, while carriers are booking freight from Singapore to JNPA at about $3,400/40ft, 5% lower than in September. Spot rates from Hong Kong to Chennai have fallen 15%, to $3,300/40ft, the data indicates. But executives at leading intra-Asia carriers claimed the latest moderate correction should not be seen as the onset of a broader cyclical downturn as, according to them, trades from Asia to India and the Middle East still remained caught up in port challenges and delays across the region. “Our Asia-India-Middle East vessels continue to operate under a lot of operational strain on the Persian Gulf end,” one source told The Loadstar.
